cards.title: Use product-level contribution margin to decide where paid spend goes
cards.summary: Break P&L economics down to the individual product so you can move ad budget from products that would sell anyway to products that need paid help.
cards.use_when: Deciding ad budget allocation across products, or whether a hero product should receive paid spend at all
steps: Build a per-product (or per-SKU) unit economics sheet: price, variable costs, contribution margin per order — the source suggests tools like Google Sheets if you don't have this.
Separate products into those selling efficiently on paid vs those that appear to sell regardless of spend (high organic/retail sell-through, suspiciously high efficiency).
Ask the counterfactual: would these people have bought this product anyway without the ad spend? For omni-channel or large brands, this is often yes for established heroes.

If yes, pull paid spend off that product — the source's example lifts contribution margin on that order by $15–$27 by not spending — and reallocate the budget to a product that genuinely needs paid media to drive sell-through (e.g., the hoodie that isn't moving organically).
Build this product-level view into the decision-making routine, not a one-off spreadsheet.
caveats: The $15–$27 margin lift is a single worked example, not a benchmark.
Cutting spend on a product that actually was incrementally driven by ads would lose sales — validate with incrementality testing where budget justifies it.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Measurement pyramid: platform metrics, finance-grade KPIs, incrementality
cards.summary: Rank your marketing metrics in a reliability pyramid — platform ROAS/CPA at the bottom, finance-grade KPIs in the middle, incrementality testing at the top.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing which marketing metrics you report on and make budget decisions from
steps: Bottom tier: in-platform ROAS, CPA, CTR, multi-touch attribution tools (e.g., Triple Whale). Fast feedback but lowest reliability — use only for directional campaign/ad feedback inside a single platform.

Middle tier: finance-grade KPIs such as acquisition MER, blended MER, profit contribution and CAC — calculated from actual new-customer counts, actual new-customer revenue, and actual ad spend, not platform-attributed numbers.
Top tier: incrementality testing (geo holdouts) — most reliable but slow, can only be run infrequently, and needs data-science capability.
Accept the trade-off as you move up: reliability improves but speed decreases. Finance-grade metrics need longer windows before you act on their movements.
The source says incrementality testing is likely not applicable to ~80% of operators; it matters mainly for businesses spending over roughly $10M/month, omni-channel or multi-market.
Never compare ROAS across platforms (e.g., Google campaign vs Meta campaign) — different attribution models and funnel positions make the numbers non-comparable.
caveats: The 80%/20% and $10M/month figures are the source's heuristics for who needs incrementality testing, not a hard rule.
The source explicitly warns against building DIY geo holdouts without proper data-science test design.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Why platform ROAS misleads: all attribution is correlation
cards.summary: Platform attribution connects correlated events, not causation, and systematically over-credits bottom-of-funnel — so ROAS misleads budget decisions.
cards.use_when: Interpreting channel-level ROAS reports or defending/attacking a channel's budget based on platform numbers
steps: Recognise that an ad click followed by a purchase is correlation, not proven causation — the source's analogy is ice cream sales and swimming deaths both rising in summer.
Account for the funnel sequence: billboard/TV/influencer creates awareness, a Meta ad 'closes' the sale, and only the Meta click gets attributed. Top-of-funnel gets no credit.

Look for the TikTok→Meta→Google pattern: TikTok drives new-market impressions without much click-off, Meta retargets and captures the demand in-platform, Google captures branded search. Increasing TikTok spend raises Meta and Google ROAS, not TikTok's.
Do not let a C-suite reader use raw cross-platform ROAS to cut TikTok and pile into Google — that removes top-of-funnel generation, and bottom-of-funnel stops working without it.
Use platform ROAS only within a platform (e.g., two Meta campaigns side by side) for directional reads.
caveats: The TikTok→Meta→Google dynamic is explicitly framed as a current, possibly time-dependent observation for some large retail brands, not a universal law.
The source notes other attribution limitations exist beyond those covered.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Use finance-grade KPIs instead of platform-attributed numbers
cards.summary: Acquisition MER, blended MER, profit contribution and CAC calculate from actual new-customer revenue and actual ad spend, making them more reliable than platform metrics.
cards.use_when: Choosing which marketing efficiency numbers to report and act on for budget decisions
steps: Acquisition MER = new-customer revenue ÷ ad spend. New-customer revenue ÷ ad spend — the source's example yields 1.4 from $100 revenue and $50 spend (reported as the multiple, not the percentage form).
Calculate from actual financial records: real new-customer counts, real new-customer revenue, real ad spend — not from platform attribution.
Do not rely on the blended MER (total revenue ÷ ad spend) for indexing paid media performance — it includes returning-customer revenue that would have returned anyway.
Always delineate finance-grade metrics into new-customer-based versions. If blended MER is 2 but new-customer MER is 1.4, the acquisition strategy may not be profitable at all.
Expect these KPIs to move slower than platform metrics — read them over longer periods before acting.
caveats: The source flags being hesitant about including MER precisely because of the returning-customer contamination problem.
The example numbers ($100 revenue, $50 spend, 1.4 new-customer MER) are illustrative calculations.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Benchmark LTGP:CAC at fixed time horizons
cards.summary: LTGP to CAC contextualises acquisition cost with customer gross profit — but must be time-boxed (30, 90, sometimes 365 days) to avoid overspending on distant lifetime value.
cards.use_when: Setting acquisition efficiency targets or auditing whether your CAC is defensible
steps: LTGP:CAC = gross profit per customer ÷ cost to acquire that customer. Example: $100 GP ÷ $33 CAC = 3.33.
Never use an unrestricted lifetime value window — the source warns that value measured across years can cause overspending on cash you won't realise for 4+ years.
Measure across two horizons: 30-day LTGP:CAC and 90-day LTGP:CAC; add 365-day only where the acquisition strategy is aggressive.

Interpret the bands as the source's heuristics: below 1.0 means losing money on acquisition — the source says most audited brands here lack the retention to support it and it's usually poor acquisition efficiency, not a strategy. 1.0–2.0 is also generally not a good position, tolerable mainly for CPG with genuinely excellent retention or when investor-funded growth throttling is required.
2.0–3.0 is the optimal zone to scale budgets. Above 3.0 is also a mistake per the source — leaving money on the table by under-leveraging paid media.
To hit the bottom of the optimal range: take first-purchase gross profit and divide by 2 — $100 GP implies $50 target CAC.
caveats: The 1/2/3 bands are the source's stated benchmarks, not a derived formula.
Below-1 performance can stem from thin gross profit (source suggests under ~$70 GP on first order is likely a problem) rather than CAC alone.
The source notes most operators overestimate their retention quality and that 0.01% of brands can genuinely operate below 1.0.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Exclude view-through conversions and existing customers from platform reporting
cards.summary: View-through conversions and existing-customer spend inflate platform ROAS — use 7-day click and check audience breakdowns and frequency.
cards.use_when: Configuring Meta attribution settings or auditing where ad budget is being spent
steps: Use 7-day click (not view-through) as the optimisation and reporting window on Meta. The source says 7-day click ROAS is highly correlated with acquisition MER in most businesses.
Understand view-through: a user sees the ad, doesn't click, buys within 24 hours, and Meta claims the conversion — many of these buyers would have bought anyway (often existing customers).
Break down by audience segments to see how much spend goes to existing customers.

Pull the frequency column and ensure 7-day frequency is under 8 — above 8 the source says you are definitely overspending because you are serving existing customers more than eight times a month, which isn't incremental.
Remember the platform incentive: platforms favour existing-customer spend and expanding attribution windows because over-attribution drives more spend.
caveats: The frequency ceiling of 8 is the source's stated heuristic.
Correlation between 7-day click ROAS and acquisition MER is stated as typical ('in most businesses'), not guaranteed.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Budget existing-customer retargeting from customer count × frequency, not a % of spend
cards.summary: Calculate existing-customer ad spend from number of existing customers × desired frequency × CPM rather than targeting a percentage of total budget.
cards.use_when: Setting retargeting/existing-customer budgets or responding to the question 'what % should go to existing customers?'
steps: Reject the percentage-allocation framing — the source calls it a bad way to look at the problem, because brands with 80% of revenue from existing customers would derive an unmanageable percentage.
Formula: existing customers × desired monthly frequency × CPM = required monthly spend.
Example: 300,000 existing customers × 3 exposures × $2.50 CPM = $2,250/month.
Get the CPM from the platform's audience segment breakdown for existing customers — the source notes $2.50 is unrealistically low and real CPMs will be higher.
Change the variables (customer count, frequency 3–6, actual CPM) to get your spend figure.

Expect the result to be far lower than intuition suggests — the source reports large brands assuming hundreds of thousands per month when $10k–$40k at a 3–6 frequency is typically sufficient, and has seen tiny businesses spending $40k/month on existing customers.
caveats: The $2.50 CPM example is fabricated for illustration.
The source states the amount needed is typically much less than operators assume, but exact figures depend on your CPM and list size.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: The profit frontier: solve for the next best dollar
cards.summary: Allocate spend by finding the marginal return of the next $10,000 on each channel, and stop each channel where incremental acquisition MER hits break-even.
cards.use_when: Deciding incremental budget allocation across channels or whether to pull budget from one channel into another
steps: Frame the question as: if we spend an extra $10,000 next month, where does it get the best incremental impact?

For each primary channel (Meta, Google, TikTok), estimate the revenue return of an additional $10,000 on top of current spend — ideally via controlled incrementality tests, or intuitively over time for seven-figure brands.
Run the inverse too: could $10,000 pulled from Google and reallocated to Meta return better (e.g., 2x on the marginal Google dollar vs 4x on new-customer revenue on Meta)?
Push each channel up to the point where it makes no more profit past that marginal dollar — the profit frontier is where incremental acquisition MER reaches break-even, and that's where you stop.
Only after reaching the profit frontier on your three primary channels should you add tertiary channels.
Avoid spreading spend across many tertiary channels before the primaries are maxed out.
caveats: The source says the only way to truly understand marginal returns is incrementality testing; intuition or marketing-mix models are substitutes at lower revenue thresholds.
The 2x/4x figures are illustrative of the reallocation logic, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Grade inventory to drive paid-media decisions on slow-moving stock
cards.summary: Grade inventory A–D by sell-through and use paid media to liquidate grade B/C/D stock back into cash — a job profit-KPI'd agencies often ignore.
cards.use_when: Planning product launches, SKU rationalisation, or deciding whether to push clearance inventory through ads at break-even or a slight loss
steps: Grade inventory by movement: A = fast-moving (focus on not going out of stock), B = medium/low sell-through, C/D = barely or not moving.
Check Shopify's auto-ranked inventory grades (source points to the Products tab; verify current interface location).
When a launch lands in C/D (the source's example: $1M ordered, only $100k sold, 400 days of cover), calculate days of inventory on hand and prioritise turning it back into cash.

Use paid media deliberately on C/D stock: dedicate it its own isolated ad funnel (it doesn't have to sit on the main site), use whitelisting pages, or push it into a new country where heavy discounting won't erode brand equity in the primary market.
Accept break-even or slight-loss selling on dead stock as a cash-conversion decision, not a profit decision.
Rationalise SKU count as new products are introduced so inventory on the balance sheet doesn't keep growing.
Give the paid media team visibility of inventory grades — the source warns agencies KPI'd purely on profit will starve grade B/C/D inventory of spend.
caveats: Source notes most brands cannot reposition a single product into a large TAM the way supplement brands (Grenade, AG1, IM8) can, so product launches are needed — and many fail.
The $1M/400-days figures are illustrative.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Cash conversion cycle explains why ecommerce can't scale arbitrarily fast
cards.summary: CCC (DIIO + DSO − DPO) plus supplier lead time and payment terms caps real growth speed regardless of ad efficiency.
cards.use_when: Setting growth targets, planning purchase orders, or evaluating whether rapid ad-spend scaling is fundable
steps: Formula: cash conversion cycle = days inventory outstanding + days sales outstanding − days payable outstanding.
Work through the compounding: if $50 gross profit lets you buy 11 units next cycle and yields $55, which buys 12, inventory purchasing grows only incrementally off prior gross profit.
Add supplier lead time — e.g., a 90-day lead time with full upfront payment means you must fund inventory 90 days before selling it, potentially forcing a 90-day stockout while waiting for cash.

Levers to fix it: negotiate better supplier terms (e.g., only 20% upfront, paying the balance on shipment — the source's example reduces stockout from 90 days to ~20), reduce lead time via a different manufacturer, or use inventory financing.
Recognise the risk of inventory financing: expensive, usually requires personal collateral, and depends on selling future units at an efficiency that can repay the loan.
caveats: The source recommends dedicated resources for calculating and benchmarking CCC rather than relying on the overview here.

The source reports seeing seven-figure businesses tripling spend from $20k to $200k/month via agency work, funded by millions in inventory financing, ending with net margin squeezed near zero after interest and marketing-efficiency compression — an observation, not a benchmark.
The source's judgement that tripling an ecommerce business in a year is not possible is attributed to them.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Resolve the CFO vs CMO spend-cut reflex with inventory reality
cards.summary: When unsold inventory is stuck, cutting media can deepen a revenue decline — sometimes the correct move is to raise MAR temporarily to liquidate stock.
cards.use_when: Responding to a cash squeeze or a CFO request to cut marketing budget when inventory isn't selling
steps: Recognise the typical scenario: inventory from November still unsold in February (some in grade C/D), so finance proposes cutting media spend ~40% to preserve cash.

Understand why the P&L reflex fires: revenue dips, marketing as a percentage spikes (e.g., from 25% to 30%), profitability falls (e.g., from 30% to 25%), and finance concludes marketing has got out of control.
Check first whether marketing is actually driving the revenue. If media spend is cut, revenue dips further, and the cuts become cyclical — less spend, less revenue, lower profit, more cuts.

Consider the counterintuitive fix: increase marketing spend in the short term (source's example: deliberately lift MAR from 30% to 35%) purely to liquidate grade C/D inventory and turn it back into cash, restoring the prior revenue position faster.
Frame the decision as converting aged inventory to cash, not as an efficiency improvement.
Ensure marketing and finance have shared visibility of inventory grades so this conversation happens before the squeeze.
caveats: The 40%/25–30%/35% figures are the source's illustrative example.
The source frames the CFO's initial reaction as logical from the P&L alone — the issue is context the P&L doesn't show.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Forecast new-customer and returning-customer revenue separately
cards.summary: Forecast new and returning revenue as separate models because they have different underlying inputs — spend-driven vs cohort/event-driven.
cards.use_when: Building an ecommerce revenue forecast, budget or KPI target
steps: Rule one of DTC forecasting per the source: always forecast new-customer revenue separately from returning-customer revenue.
New-customer revenue is driven primarily by marketing inputs: ad spend, plus events and influencers where applicable, plus any tertiary channels.

Returning-customer revenue is driven by product launches, marketing events (e.g., discount periods), direct channels (email/SMS) and other reasons for customers to come back — ad spend contributes only a little.
Practise input-based forecasting: forecast the inputs (spend, launch calendar, events) and derive the output, rather than extrapolating the revenue line directly.
Look backwards at inputs to justify the number, not just at last period's revenue.
caveats: The delineation is the source's stated cardinal rule for DTC forecasting.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Build returning-customer forecasts from cohort repeat rates
cards.summary: Project next month's returning revenue by ageing every historical new-customer cohort through its average repeat rate and returning AOV, then adjusting for seasonality and events.
cards.use_when: Forecasting returning-customer revenue for next month's budget or board plan
steps: Build a cohort table of new customers acquired each month going back to your earliest data (e.g., Jan 2021 onward).
Derive the repeat rate by customer age: e.g., 7% in month 1, 6%, 4%, 2%, 1%, tapering to a small asymptote.

For each cohort, take its original new-customer count, apply the average repeat rate for the month it is about to enter (e.g., month 32 ≈ 0.1%), then multiply by returning-customer AOV (e.g., $100 → 100 × 0.1% × $100 = $1).
Sum across every cohort to get the returning-customer revenue expectation for next month.
Expect this method to land within roughly 10% accuracy on its own.

To tighten to 1–2% accuracy: (1) apply a seasonality factor from the last 3 years of returning-customer revenue seasonality, and (2) superimpose planned marketing events/product launches with their expected revenue realisation.
caveats: The 10% and 1–2% accuracy figures are the source's reported outcomes, not guarantees.
Requires sufficient cohort history to extrapolate old cohorts.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Model new-customer revenue by regression of spend vs acquisition MER
cards.summary: Plot daily spend against acquisition MER, strip outlier periods, fit a regression, and back-propagate from the new-customer revenue goal to see whether it's achievable.
cards.use_when: Forecasting new-customer revenue at a given spend level, or sanity-checking a growth target
steps: Plot daily data for the last year or so: acquisition MER on the y-axis, spend on the x-axis.
Fit a logarithmic or linear regression (whichever fits best) to get expected efficiency at a given spend level.

Remove outliers before fitting: sales periods, Black Friday/November periods (they overstate BAU efficiency), and any low-spend days below the minimum you'd realistically run (source's example: exclude days under $1,000).
Read the fitted line to answer: at $8,000/day, roughly what efficiency should we expect?

Back-propagate from the goal: for a target of, say, $100,000 new-customer revenue at 4x acquisition MER, go to 4 on the graph and read across to find the required spend — then check whether that spend is feasible.
If the answer is no, identify the actual input or lever that will beat last year's average: a marketing event, a new product launch, a new channel, or a step change in creative production.
Treat the gap between realistic expectation and target as the central forecasting exercise — there will always be a delta.
caveats: Other channels (influencers, etc.) require bespoke modelling rather than this paid-ads regression.
The source frames this level of modelling as critical at 8–9 figure scale; smaller brands may use simpler approaches.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Don't overallocate to bottom-of-funnel because it shows the best ROAS
cards.summary: Bottom-of-funnel campaigns always show the best platform ROAS and top-of-funnel the worst, so shifting budget toward the 6x and away from the 2x usually reduces incremental growth.
cards.use_when: Reallocating budget between campaigns or channels based on platform ROAS reads
steps: Expect the pattern: bottom-of-funnel (retargeting, branded search) will always attribute highest; top-of-funnel will attribute lowest.
When you see Meta at 2x and Google at 6x, do not simply move budget to Google — the source says the 6x is likely over-attributing because of its funnel position, branded terms, or retargeting.
Assume better incremental impact likely sits further up funnel, even with weaker in-platform numbers.
Validate only within a controlled test if you are making a significant reallocation, and check whether the pattern holds for your specific business.
If you increase budgets into bottom-of-funnel on the strength of its ROAS, expect non-growth — the source describes this as a common mistake.
caveats: The source says 'likely' and 'probably' — the bottom-of-funnel over-attribution is a tendency, not a certainty, and should be verified with testing per business.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Allocate part of marketing expense to brand, not just performance
cards.summary: Beyond roughly $1M–20M, performance marketing alone hits diminishing returns; brand associations built outside the ad account are what keep ad-account metrics strong at scale.
cards.use_when: Setting overall marketing budget allocation or planning acquisition strategy past a performance plateau
steps: Recognise the plateau: as daily ad spend pushes past roughly $30k–$40k/day, performance marketing alone stops getting further, per the source's stated experience.

Understand why large brands (e.g., $300M/year) can show better CPMs, CTRs, CPCs, CVRs and ROAS than $8M/year brands at 20x the volume: market saturation and associations built outside the ad account make the in-platform metrics look good.
Budget explicitly for branding efforts as a line on the P&L — associations in market delivered where your customers already are: events, areas, creators and content they consume.
Do not expect individual brand activations to show directly profitable ROI; the effect is the overarching association driving purchases that won't be attributed to performance campaigns.

The source's examples: buying running gear because every running influencer followed wears the brand; buying premium activewear because of a perception of quality built through creative and campaign shoots, not product experience at purchase.
caveats: The $1M–$20M brute-force range and the $30k–$40k/day plateau are the source's stated observations, not hard thresholds.
Individual brand activations likely won't show direct profitable ROI — the source says this is expected and accepted.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Know your gross margin and variable costs as the base of all finance decisions
cards.summary: The source's first key takeaway: understand gross margin, how to calculate it correctly, and the difference between product margin and gross margin.
cards.use_when: Reviewing unit economics, setting pricing or acquisition targets, or preparing a P&L for a marketing decision
steps: Identify all variable costs that belong in the margin calculation, not just product cost.
Distinguish product margin from gross margin — the source calls this a required distinction and lists it as takeaway number one.
Use the corrected gross margin as the basis for downstream metrics: contribution margin by product, CAC targets, LTGP:CAC, and profit contribution.
Check whether thin first-order gross profit is the real constraint on acquisition (the source flags under roughly $70 GP on first order as likely a problem), rather than immediately blaming CAC.
caveats: The source lists this as one of five closing takeaways and does not detail the full variable-cost build-up in this section.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx
